Consult Summary:
- Progressive exertional dyspnea over ~2 weeks with new bilateral ankle swelling in a patient with known heart failure; clinical picture most consistent with acute decompensated chronic heart failure. Vitals and chest exam reportedly stable.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline: Shortness of breath gradually worsening over the last couple of weeks; markedly worse in the past few days. Now breathless with minimal exertion/around the house; previously able to walk to the shops without issue.
- Associated symptoms: Mild dry cough; bilateral ankle swelling for a few days; feels a bit run-down.
- Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, palpitations, fever. Appetite and oral intake OK. Urinating frequently (baseline on diuretics).
- Past medical history: Chronic heart failure; prior “small heart attack” (likely myocardial infarction) ~5 years ago; no other conditions reported.
- Medications: Furosemide (dose unknown; previously once daily); Aspirin; Bisoprolol. 
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction in early 60s; mother has osteoporosis.
- Social: Lives alone with two cats; part-time lorry (truck) driver (day shifts); former smoker (~1 pack/day for ~25 years); no alcohol; limited exercise (walks to shops).

Examination:
- Per clinician report: Chest exam normal; oxygen saturation OK; blood pressure OK (no numeric values provided).
- No additional physical findings documented beyond patient-reported ankle swelling.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute decompensated chronic heart failure (volume overload) — high likelihood. Supported by known HF, progressive exertional dyspnea, and new bilateral ankle edema; previous improvement on diuretic; vitals stable do not exclude decompensation.
- Additional considerations (from DDx):
  - Anemia contributing to dyspnea/HF decompensation — medium likelihood (fatigue/run-down; CBC planned).
  - Arrhythmia precipitating HF decompensation (e.g., atrial fibrillation) — medium-low likelihood (can be asymptomatic; no palpitations reported; vitals “OK”).
  - Less likely: Pulmonary embolism, COPD exacerbation (gradual course, normal saturations, bilateral edema favor HF).

Plan:
- Medications: Increase furosemide from once daily to twice daily for the next few days to improve diuresis; reassess response.
- Tests:
  - Blood tests: CBC (evaluate for anemia); renal function/electrolytes (monitor diuretic impact).
  - Echocardiogram to reassess cardiac function (to be scheduled; may take 1–2 weeks).
  - Additional considerations consistent with DDx: Obtain ECG to assess rhythm; consider thyroid function testing if clinically indicated.
- Follow-up: Return in ~1 week for review of symptoms and test results.
- Safety-net: Seek earlier evaluation if worsening breathlessness, development of chest pain, palpitations, or dizziness.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - Objective vital sign values (BP, HR, SpO2), weight and recent weight change.
  - Detailed respiratory exam findings (rales/wheeze), JVP, objective exam of edema.
  - Orthopnea/paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea history; cough sputum character; sleep quality.
  - Exact medication doses and full medication reconciliation; adherence assessment.
  - Baseline HF metrics (prior echocardiogram/EF), vaccination status, and dietary/fluid/sodium guidance.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant. Brief medication name confusion (metoprolol vs bisoprolol) resolved by patient confirming bisoprolol.
● Transcript quality:
  - Adequate but limited detail; some audio/connection issues; examination findings referenced without numeric values; medication doses unspecified.
